title: When Drinking Coffee Was Punishable by Death
hook: Sultan Murad IV banned coffee and executed anyone caught sipping it.

scenes.text: In the 16th century, coffee arrived in Istanbul from Yemen, igniting a craze for public 'kahvehane' coffeehouses.

scenes.text: Unlike quiet mosques, coffeehouses buzzed with poets, chess players, political gossip, and fierce debates about government policy.

scenes.text: Sultans viewed these caffeine-fueled debates as dangerous breeding grounds for treason, revolution, and military coups.

scenes.text: In 1633, Sultan Murad IV strictly banned coffee and tobacco across the entire empire under penalty of immediate public execution.
scenes.imagePrompt: Imperial Ottoman decree parchment with red and gold royal tughra seal nailed onto a wooden public notice board. 2D flat cartoon illustration, thick dark outlines, warm muted palette, hand-painted textures, vertical 9:16, no people in the foreground, no text, no logos
scenes.voicedText: In 1633, Sultan Murad IV strictly banned coffee and tobacco across the entire empire under penalty of immediate public execution.

scenes.text: Murad disguised himself as a common beggar and stalked Istanbul taverns at night, beheading illicit coffee drinkers on the spot.

scenes.voicedText: Murad disguised himself as a common beggar and stalked Istanbul taverns at night, beheading illicit coffee drinkers on the spot.

scenes.text: Despite the brutal ban, the love for coffee was unstoppable, and later Sultans taxed coffee instead. Could you give up coffee on pain of death?
